newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-NEW U.S. OPEN STADIUM NAMED AFTER ARTHUR ASHE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-NEW U.S. OPEN STADIUM NAMED AFTER ARTHUR ASHE.

text.p: The new stadium that will serve as centre stage for the U.S. Open championships starting next summer will be named Arthur Ashe Stadium, the United States Tennis Association announced on Wednesday.

The 23,000-seat stadium, centrepiece of a $234 million expansion project of the National Tennis Centre at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park, honours the former U.S. Open, Australian Open and Wimbledon champion, who died of AIDS in 1993.

The announcement was made at an emotional news conference led by USTA President Harry Marmion and attended by Ashe's widow, Jeanne Moutoussamy-Ashe, and New York mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who saluted human rights activist Ashe as a "hero."
Marmion sobbed as he made the official declaration. "For generations to come, marquee matches will be played with players from all over the world," he said, breaking into tears.
"Arthur Ashe was a great humanitarian and a great tennis player and a role model for people around the world."
Ashe contracted the AIDS virus through a blood transfusion while undergoing surgery in 1988.

The announcement ended months of speculation about the naming of the new facility, which had appeared set to be dubbed USTA Stadium. The USTA Board of Directors, last weekend in Atlanta, decided unanimously, Marmion said, to honour Ashe.
Said Moutoussamy-Ashe, "I'm elated about the tribute here today for Arthur. Tomorrow would have been our 20th wedding anniversary, and this is a wonderful gift in honour for our entire family."
"Arthur Ashe Stadium is a lasting tribute to Arthur and a meaningful committment to his values and embodies his contributions as a leader, humanitarian, educator and athlete."
"We are enormously proud of you, Arthur."

Ashe became the first African American man to win a Grand Slam title when he captured the 1968 U.S. Open, the first of the open era, as an amateur. He later won the Australian Open in 1970 and Wimbledon in 1975 and finished his career with 33 career titles.
After his playing days, Ashe captained the U.S. Davis Cup team, leading the Americans to two titles.

He also championed junior tennis programmes, particularly for minority youth, and was an outspoken opponent of apartheid in South Africa. Away from the court, Ashe also compiled a three-volume series on the history of blacks in sport.

Ashe attended his final U.S. Open in 1992. The day before the tournament, many top players took part in a fund-raising exhibition benefitting the Arthur Ashe Foundation for the Defeat of AIDS. The exhibition has become an annual event.

Said Mayor Giuliani: "It is a pleasure to join all of you today for this official announcement that the new stadium, the main court at the USTA National Tennis Centre from now until forever will be named for a great hero.

"Arthur Ashe was one of our greatest athletes but that was only part of the tremendous contribution that he made. He was an outstanding citizen and a person who was a leader for all of the very best things."
